title: Green Hydrogen in North Africa: Morocco, Egypt, Mauritania and the Missing Buyers | The Six, Ep. 17
lede: Morocco, Egypt and Mauritania have lined up projects and agreements valued at tens of billions of dollars to turn sun and wind into hydrogen and ammonia for export. But Africa makes only about 6,000 tonnes of low-emissions hydrogen today, and the IEA counts at most one of the continent's projects for 2030 with a final investment decision.
keyPoints: Africa produces about 6,000 tonnes of low-emissions hydrogen a year. Projects planned for 2030 would make 1.2 million tonnes, but at most one has reached a final investment decision (IEA, Global Hydrogen Review 2026).

In March 2025, Morocco picked five consortia for six projects under its Morocco Offer, with 319 billion dirhams (about $32 billion) of planned investment. Investors received land reservation agreements in February 2026 (MAP; Morocco World News).

Egypt's flagship project at Ain Sokhna pairs a 100 MW electrolyser with Fertiglobe's ammonia plant, for up to 74,000 tonnes of green ammonia a year. Germany's H2Global agreed to buy at €1,000 a tonne; the investment decision, once expected in 2025, is still pending (Ammonia Energy Association; S&P Global).

On Sept. 16, 2026, Mauritania signed a convention with CWP Global for the AMAN project: up to 18 GW of renewable power and about 1.2 million tonnes of green hydrogen a year, with a final investment decision targeted before 2030 (Latham & Watkins).
The constraint is buyers: worldwide, only about 20% of newly signed hydrogen offtake volumes were firm commitments (IEA).
